items.title: Oslo and the Palestinian Authority
items.sum: Israel and the PLO recognised each other and set up the Palestinian Authority to run parts of Gaza and Judea and Samaria for an interim period. The final issues were left for later talks, which failed at Camp David in 2000.
items.detail:
Recognition: On 9 September 1993 Israel and the PLO exchanged letters of mutual recognition, and on 13 September Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat signed the Declaration of Principles (Oslo I) at the White House.

The PA: The Cairo agreement of 4 May 1994 created the Palestinian Authority and handed it Gaza and Jericho. The Oslo II agreement of 28 September 1995 extended its rule to the main Palestinian towns of Judea and Samaria. Arafat was elected PA president in January 1996.

Left for later: Jerusalem, refugees, borders, security and Israeli communities were left for final-status talks, due to end by May 1999.

Violence: Hamas and Islamic Jihad opposed the accords and carried out suicide bombings in Israeli cities. On 4 November 1995 Rabin was murdered in Tel Aviv by an Israeli opponent of the accords.

Camp David: In July 2000 a summit between Ehud Barak and Arafat, hosted by President Clinton, ended without agreement.

items.title: The Second Intifada
items.sum: An armed uprising with waves of suicide bombings in Israeli cities. Israel retook the Palestinian towns in 2002 and began building a security barrier.
items.detail:
Start: Riots broke out at the end of September 2000, after Ariel Sharon visited the Temple Mount on 28 September, and quickly turned into armed attacks.

Suicide bombings: Hamas, Islamic Jihad and Fatah's armed wing carried out scores of suicide bombings on buses, restaurants and hotels. On 27 March 2002 a bomber killed 30 people at a Passover meal at the Park Hotel in Netanya.

Defensive Shield: Two days later Israel launched Operation Defensive Shield and retook the cities of Judea and Samaria, besieging Arafat's compound in Ramallah. In June 2002 Israel decided to build a security barrier.

The toll: About 1,000 Israelis and about 3,000 Palestinians were killed.

The end: Arafat died on 11 November 2004. Mahmoud Abbas was elected PA president on 9 January 2005, and at Sharm el-Sheikh on 8 February 2005 he and Sharon declared an end to the violence.

items.title: The disengagement from Gaza
items.sum: Israel removed all 21 of its communities in Gaza and four in northern Samaria, and pulled its army out of the Strip.
items.detail:
The plan: Prime Minister Ariel Sharon announced the plan in December 2003. The Knesset approved it in October 2004 and passed the law in February 2005.

The evacuation: From 15 August 2005 about 8,000 Israeli citizens were moved out of Gush Katif and the other communities in Gaza, and of four communities in northern Samaria (Ganim, Kadim, Homesh and Sa-Nur). The houses were demolished.

The pullout: The last soldiers left Gaza on 12 September 2005. Israel kept control of Gaza's airspace, sea and most of its crossings; Egypt controlled the Rafah crossing with EU monitors from November 2005.

items.title: Hamas wins and takes Gaza: the split
items.sum: Hamas won the 2006 parliamentary election and in June 2007 took Gaza by force from Fatah. Since then Hamas has ruled Gaza and the PA has ruled the Palestinian towns of Judea and Samaria.
items.detail:
The election: On 25 January 2006 Hamas won 74 of the 132 seats in the Palestinian Legislative Council; Fatah won 45. It was the last national Palestinian election.

Conditions: The Quartet (the US, EU, UN and Russia) said aid depended on Hamas recognising Israel, renouncing violence and accepting past agreements. Hamas refused.

Shalit: On 25 June 2006 Hamas and other groups crossed from Gaza and captured soldier Gilad Shalit. He was held until October 2011, when he was exchanged for 1,027 Palestinian prisoners, among them Yahya Sinwar.

The takeover: After months of fighting between the two movements, Hamas took full control of Gaza on 14–15 June 2007. Abbas dismissed the Hamas-led government and appointed a new one in Ramallah. Israel and Egypt tightened control of Gaza's crossings, and Israel declared Gaza a hostile entity in September 2007. Later unity deals were never carried out.

items.title: The Gaza rounds
items.sum: Rocket fire from Gaza led to four large Israeli operations, each ended by an Egyptian-brokered truce, with smaller rounds in between.
items.detail:
Cast Lead: From 27 December 2008 to 18 January 2009 Israel fought in Gaza by air and, from 3 January, on the ground, to stop rocket fire. 13 Israelis were killed; Palestinian counts were about 1,400.

Pillar of Defense: From 14 to 21 November 2012, after Israel killed Hamas's military commander Ahmed Jabari, an eight-day air campaign. Iron Dome intercepted rockets fired at Tel Aviv and Jerusalem for the first time.

Protective Edge: From 8 July to 26 August 2014, after the kidnapping and murder of three Israeli teenagers in Gush Etzion in June, a 50-day war with a ground operation against Hamas's cross-border tunnels. 67 Israeli soldiers and 6 civilians in Israel were killed; Palestinian counts were about 2,250. Hamas took the bodies of soldiers Hadar Goldin and Oron Shaul.

Guardian of the Walls: From 10 to 21 May 2021, after unrest in Jerusalem, Hamas fired rockets at Jerusalem and about 4,300 rockets were fired at Israel in 11 days. Riots broke out in mixed Jewish-Arab cities in Israel.

Between rounds: Smaller rounds, mostly with Islamic Jihad, came in 2019, 2022 (Breaking Dawn) and May 2023 (Shield and Arrow). Israel allowed Qatari cash and work permits into Gaza.

items.title: Areas A, B and C, and the Israeli communities
items.sum: The Oslo II agreement split Judea and Samaria into three areas. Israel has full control of Area C, about 60% of the land, where the Israeli communities are.
items.detail:
Area A: About 18% of the land, the main Palestinian cities. The PA runs civil affairs and security, though the IDF enters for raids.

Area B: About 22%, mostly Palestinian villages. The PA runs civil affairs; Israel controls security.

Area C: About 60%, including the Jordan Valley, open land and the Israeli communities. Israel controls security and planning, through the Civil Administration under COGAT.

The communities: Israel built communities in Judea and Samaria after 1967. About half a million Israeli citizens live there, not counting the Jerusalem neighbourhoods beyond the 1967 line. Most countries regard the communities as illegal under international law; Israel disputes this. Outposts built without government approval are illegal under Israeli law too, though governments have legalised some.

Hebron: Under a 1997 protocol, Hebron is split into H1 (PA) and H2 (Israeli control), which includes the Jewish quarter and the Cave of the Patriarchs.

items.title: UNRWA and the refugee question
items.sum: UNRWA is the UN agency for Palestinian refugees and their descendants, who it says now number about 5.9 million. Israel accuses it of being infiltrated by Hamas.
items.detail:
The refugees: About 700,000 Arabs fled or were driven out of what became Israel in the 1947–49 war. Palestinians call it the Nakba and demand a right of return; Israel rejects return to Israel, saying it would end Israel as a Jewish state.

The agency: The UN General Assembly set up UNRWA in December 1949, and it began work in 1950. Unlike other refugees, the status passes to descendants. UNRWA runs schools, clinics and camps in Gaza, Judea and Samaria, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria. Most people in Gaza are registered refugees.

The dispute: Israel says Hamas uses UNRWA buildings and that hundreds of its staff are members of armed groups; UNRWA denies systematic ties.

The Timeline: The charges over 7 October and the Knesset ban on UNRWA are in Khan Younis and Rafah, and Philadelphi, Netzarim and the killing of Sinwar.

items.title: Jerusalem and the Temple Mount status quo
items.sum: Israel took East Jerusalem in 1967 and calls the whole city its capital. On the Temple Mount, Muslims pray and Jews may visit but not pray, under a status quo Israel says it keeps.
items.detail:
The city: Israel took East Jerusalem and the Old City from Jordan in the Six-Day War of June 1967 and applied its law there. The 1980 Basic Law declared 'Jerusalem, complete and united' the capital of Israel. Palestinians want East Jerusalem as their capital. The US recognised Jerusalem as Israel's capital in December 2017 and moved its embassy there in May 2018.

The Temple Mount: The site is Judaism's holiest, where the two Temples stood, and holds the al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock, Islam's third-holiest site. After 1967 Defense Minister Moshe Dayan left it under the Jordanian-run Islamic Waqf.

The status quo: Muslims may pray there; non-Muslims, including Jews, may visit at set times but may not pray. Israel's police control access. Jordan's special role was confirmed in the 1994 peace treaty. In recent years more Jews have visited and some have prayed quietly; Israel's government says the status quo has not changed.

Flashpoints: Clashes on the Mount set off wider violence in 2000, 2017 and 2021.
